Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). # Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey

About the Survey

Purpose

The Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MARTS) provides an early indication of sales of retail and food service companies. It was developed in response to requests by government, business, and other users to provide an early indication of current retail trade activity in the United States. Retail sales are one of the primary measures of consumer demand for both durable and non-durable goods. MARTS also provides an estimate of monthly sales at food service establishments and drinking places.

Coverage

Retail and food service companies with one or more establishments that sell merchandise and associated services to final consumers (NAICS Sector 44-45 & Sector 72, subsector 722). During 2012, monthly retail and food service sales ranged from $358 billion to $469 billion.

Content

Companies provide data on dollar value of sales, reporting period, and number of retail establishments.

Frequency

Monthly since 1953; except for February 1970 to February 1972. Reported data are for activity taking place during the previous month. Forms are mailed 5 working days before the end of the reporting month and responses are due 2 working days after the reporting month. Smaller and medium sized retailers participate in the survey for about two years and then are replaced with new firms.

Methods

A mail-out/mail-back survey of a sub-sample of companies and Employer Identification Numbers (EINs) selected from the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS). The advance survey sample of about 4,800 firms is selected by stratifying the companies in the larger MRTS sample by major kind-of-business and sales size and selecting the desired number of cases within each size stratum using a systematic probability-proportional-to-size procedure where the size used is the MRTS sampling weight. Some 1,150 firms, because of their relatively large effect on the sales of certain industry groups, are selected with certainty.

Advance sales estimates for each kind of business are developed by applying a ratio of current-month to previous-month sales (derived from the advance retail and food service sample) to the preliminary estimate of sales for the previous month (from the larger monthly sample). Industry estimates are summed to derive total retail sales figures. Data are seasonally adjusted. Publication of the advance report was suspended in the 1970's because of unsatisfactory relationships between the advance and later monthly estimates, and was resumed after modification of the estimating procedure. Numerous improvements to the estimation procedure have been made since then and the average absolute revision to the advance estimate is now two-tenths of one percent.

Products

Advance Monthly Retail Sales reports are released about 9 working days after the close of the reference month. They contain the advance estimates for the reporting month and preliminary sales data for the previous month by major kind-of-business group. Data presented are both seasonally adjusted and unadjusted.

Uses

This economic indicator is widely used and closely watched throughout government, academic, and business communities. The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses the estimates as an input for estimating Gross Domestic Product. The Federal Reserve Board uses the estimates to anticipate economic trends. The Council of Economic Advisors uses the estimates for economic policy analysis.

The news media report on this indicator regularly and use the estimates for economic analysis. Financial analysts and

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)
Organization/publisher: U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The U.S. Census Bureau conducts the Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS) to produce early national estimates of total and month-to-month change in sales for retail and food service establishments located in the United States. A retail establishment is one that sells merchandise to the general public (final consumers). The estimates from MARTS are released approximately ten business days after the end of the reference month and are revised one month later by estimates from the Monthly Retail Trade and Food Services Survey (MRTS). Estimates are summarized by industry classification based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively, starting with the Census Bureau's own documentation and related sources.Good foundation. Now let me dig into the survey's history, data access channels, and its users (like the Federal Reserve and BEA).Now let me look into the market impact, data access channels, and recent events like shutdowns and the nonemployer methodology change.Let me gather remaining details on data access channels (API, FRED), the COVID-19 collection challenges, and the PFEI designation.# Research Report: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)

**Report date:** October 8, 2026
**Subject:** Federal statistical dataset, U.S. Census Bureau

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is essentially accurate. I verified every element against the Census Bureau's own methodology pages, Federal Register notices, and the survey's published releases. Two minor refinements:

- **Release timing:** Census describes the advance report as released "about 9 working days after the close of the reference month" in some documentation and "approximately two weeks" / "approximately 12 days" after the reference month in OMB clearance documents. Your "approximately ten business days" is within the range Census itself uses, though official language varies between ~9 and ~12 business days depending on the document's vintage.
- The survey is also an **OMB-designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI)** — a fact worth adding to any description, as it triggers special release and pre-release-access safeguards.

Everything else — publisher, purpose, the one-month-later revision by the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS), and NAICS-based industry classification — checks out against primary sources.

---

## 2. Publisher and Institutional Context

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Publisher** | U.S. Census Bureau, an agency of the U.S. Department of Commerce |
| **Program family** | The "Monthly Retail Surveys" (MRS), comprising two surveys: the larger Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS, ~13,000 employer firms) and MARTS (a ~4,800-firm subsample of it) |
| **Product line** | Part of the Census Bureau's Economic Indicators program (alongside construction, manufacturing, wholesale trade, and international trade indicators) |
| **Contacts / pages** | Main portal: census.gov/retail; methodology: census.gov/retail/marts/how_surveys_are_collected.html; FAQ: census.gov/retail/marts_general_faqs.html |
| **OMB clearance** | OMB Control Number 0607-0104 (Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey); the combined Monthly Retail Surveys are periodically re-cleared via Federal Register notice, most recently August 5, 2025 (90 FR 37470) |

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority:** Title 13, United States Code, **Sections 131 and 182**, which authorize the Census Bureau to conduct interim economic surveys between the economic censuses and to request voluntary assistance from businesses. (Earlier OMB clearance notices cited Section 182 alone; current notices cite both 131 and 182.)
- **Confidentiality:** Title 13 U.S.C. **Section 9** obliges the Census Bureau to keep respondent data confidential and to use them only to produce statistics; individual company responses cannot be publicly released.
- **Voluntary response:** Respondent's obligation is **voluntary**, not mandatory — a notable burden consideration (see Section 10).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** The collection operates under OMB Control No. 0607-0104, with periodic public comment requests in the Federal Register (e.g., 2023-00622, 2012-15525, 2025-14783).
- **Principal Federal Economic Indicator status:** Per the 2025 Federal Register clearance notice, "MARTS provide an OMB-designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator and the earliest available monthly estimates of broad-based retail trade activity." PFEI status subjects the release to OMB statistical policy directives on timing, embargo, and pre-release access (the advance retail sales release is distributed via a **press lockup room** before the 8:30 a.m. ET release, per research on macro-news pre-release safeguards).

---

## 4. History

- **1953:** MARTS began as a monthly survey, "developed in response to requests by government, business, and other users to provide an early indication of current retail trade activity in the United States" (Federal Register, 2023). Historical press releases are archived back to **December 1953**.
- **1970–1972:** Publication of the advance report was **suspended from (approximately) March 1970 to January 1972** because of "unsatisfactory relationships between the advance and later monthly estimates," then **resumed after modification of the estimating procedure**. Census's historical release page confirms "Advance Retail Sales not produced from March 1970 to January 1972," and the About page says "Monthly since 1953; except for February 1970 to February 1972" (the exact boundary months vary slightly between Census pages).
- **Since resumption:** "Numerous improvements to the estimation procedure have been made since then and the average absolute revision to the advance estimate is now two-tenths of one percent."
- **Gaps in the archival record:** Releases are unavailable for May 1954, January 1956, August 1956, December 1958, January 1970, December 1973, and August 1991 (per Census's historic releases page) — relevant for preservationists and time-series builders.
- **Collection mode evolution:** Older methodology (captured in archived PDFs) describes mail-out/mail-back with mail, fax, or telephone follow-up; the current methodology describes collection "by internet or telephone." Forms are provided to respondents about 5 working days before the end of the reporting month; responses are due about 2 working days after the reference month ends, and collection is complete by the sixth business day.
- **Methodology milestones:** The X-12-ARIMA seasonal adjustment software was succeeded by **X-13ARIMA-SEATS** (MARTS continues to use the X-11 filter-based adjustment within it). As of the **April 2025 annual revision**, nonemployer (no-paid-employee) firms were removed from the published estimates and time series to align with the **Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES)** — a significant, deliberate **time-series break** data scientists must handle.
- **Recent disruption:** The **October–November 2025 government shutdown (43 days, the longest in history)** halted collection, processing, and publication. The September 2025 advance report, originally due October 16, was released November 25, 2025; October 2025 was released December 16, 2025; and the release calendar then ran compressed/catch-up through 2026. (A similar disruption occurred during the 2019 shutdown.)

---

## 5. What the Survey Measures (Content and Coverage)

- **Universe:** Retail and food service companies with one or more establishments selling merchandise and associated services to final consumers — **NAICS Sector 44–45 (Retail Trade)** and **Sector 72, subsector 722 (Food Services and Drinking Places)**. It covers **employer firms** only since the April 2025 revision (previously nonemployers were represented via estimation).
- **Data items:** Dollar value of total sales; **e-commerce sales** (a newer addition); the reporting period's length (4 vs. 5 weeks) and end date if not a calendar month; number of establishments covered; and whether reported figures are estimates or "book" figures.
- **Geography:** **National estimates only** — no state or local detail.
- **Scale:** During 2012, monthly retail and food services sales ranged from $358 billion to $469 billion; by 2025–2026, monthly advance totals were roughly **$730–775 billion** (e.g., August 2026: $773.9 billion, seasonally adjusted, +1.2% m/m, +6.0% y/y).
- **Products:** Advance estimates for the reference month plus (revised) preliminary estimates for the prior month, by major kind-of-business group, both seasonally adjusted and unadjusted, in millions of dollars and percent change, with 90% confidence intervals.

---

## 6. Methodology (Technical Documentation)

**Sample design**
- MARTS is a subsample of ~4,800 units (companies and EINs) drawn from the MRTS sample of ~13,000 units; units are stratified by industry (36 primary strata) and substratified by monthly sales (3–12 size substrata).
- ~1,150 firms are selected **with certainty** (weight 1) because of their outsized effect on industry estimates; other sampling weights range up to about 1,000–1,130.
- Selection is systematic probability-proportional-to-size, with the MRTS sampling weight as the size measure.
- **No business births** are added between designs; the sample is redesigned and reselected approximately every **2½–3 years** to stay representative and to rotate reporting burden off small and medium firms (which typically serve ~2 years).

**Data collection**
- Internet or telephone; follow-up begins the third business day after the reference month; collection completes by the sixth business day. Response is **voluntary**; nonrespondents are handled through estimation rather than imputation (except a small number of influential nonrespondents, whose sales may be estimated from historical performance).

**Estimation**
- Detailed-industry advance estimates use a **link-relative estimator**: a ratio of current-to-previous-month weighted sales (from matched respondents) is multiplied by the prior month's preliminary MRTS estimate; broader aggregates are sums of detailed estimates.
- Estimates are **indirectly benchmarked to annual survey estimates** via the link-relative method; the full time series undergoes annual and periodic (5-year) benchmark revisions tied to annual programs (now the AIES).
- Variances are estimated by the **random groups** method and used to flag statistically significant changes (the familiar ± percentages and asterisks in the release).

**Seasonal adjustment**
- X-13ARIMA-SEATS software using the **X-11 filter-based adjustment procedure**, adjusting for seasonal variation and holiday/trading-day differences; data are **not adjusted for price changes** (nominal dollars).

---

## 7. Release Cycle and Revision Structure

- **Advance report (MARTS):** Released ~9–12 business days after month-end, at **8:30:00 a.m. ET**, as press release "Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services" (release numbers in the CB-xx-xxx series, e.g., CB25-169). Published on a fixed schedule (see census.gov/retail/release_schedule.html) with next-release dates announced in each report.
- **One month later:** Advance estimates are superseded by "preliminary" and then "final" estimates from the larger MRTS (the full MRTS release follows about 6 weeks after the reference month).
- **Annual revisions** and **5-year benchmark revisions** to annual survey/arts-AIES levels reshape history — in April 2025, for example, the nonemployer redefinition reset the entire published time series.
- **Practical implication:** Every MARTS datum is best understood as "first-vintage" data. Related e-commerce estimates appear in the separate Quarterly Retail E-Commerce Sales report (~50 days after quarter close).

---

## 8. Data Access and Preservation Channels

**Primary/Census channels**
- Current and historical press releases (PDF): census.gov/retail/sales.html and www2.census.gov/marts/advYYMM.pdf and www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/ (archived releases back to December 1953).
- Downloadable Excel/CSV time series of advance estimates (linked from the Retail - Monthly data pages).
- **Census Bureau economic time series tool / API:** census.gov/econ/currentdata/?programCode=MARTS provides queryable, chartable, and downloadable time series (MARTS is one of the program codes in Census's economic indicator time series data services).
- Methodology documentation: census.gov/retail/marts/how_surveys_are_collected.html (plus archived PDF versions under www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/mrts/).
- Historic survey forms (for studying respondent burden and question evolution): census.gov/retail/get_forms.html → Historic Forms.

**Secondary/derived channels**
- **FRED (St. Louis Fed):** release "Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services" (release ID 9) carries dozens of series, including headline and percent-change series — e.g., RSAFS (Retail & Food Services, SA), RSAFSNA (NSA), RSXFS (Retail Trade, SA), RSFSDP (Food Services & Drinking Places), RSFSXMV (ex-motor vehicles), MARTSMPCSM44000USS (percent change, SA), and related ex-auto/ex-gas aggregates.
- **ALFRED (ArchivaL FRED):** preserves **vintage (as-first-released) versions** of these series — invaluable for studying real-time revisions and for replicating historical analysis.
- News aggregators and commercial data providers republish the release nearly in real time.

**Preservation notes**
- The press-release archive on www2.census.gov is the deep historical record (1953–present, with the noted gaps).
- The April 2025 nonemployer redefinition means older and newer vintages of the "same" series are not strictly comparable — a preservationist should retain both the vintage data (ALFRED) and Census's revision documentation.
- Shutdown-delayed releases (2019, 2025) mean some months have release dates months after their reference months — metadata capture of release dates (not just reference months) matters.

---

## 9. Typical Users and Uses

Per Census's own documentation and Federal Register justifications:

- **Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA):** Uses MARTS/MRTS estimates as a principal source for the **personal consumption expenditures (PCE) component of GDP** — the advance report is available in time to feed BEA's advance GDP estimates, with the fuller MRTS incorporated into the 2nd and 3rd estimates. BEA's NIPA Handbook explicitly names the advance retail report as a principal source.
- **Federal Reserve Board:** "Policymakers such as the Federal Reserve Board need to have the timeliest estimates in order to anticipate economic trends and act accordingly." The Chicago Fed even publishes **CARTS** (Chicago Fed Advance Retail Trade Summary), a weekly nowcast benchmarked to MARTS/MRTS.
- **Council of Economic Advisers and National Economic Council:** economic policy analysis.
- **State and federal agencies**, market research firms, and **financial analysts**: market trend analysis and economic forecasting.
- **Businesses:** benchmarking their own performance and predicting demand for their products.
- **News media:** the release is one of the most closely covered monthly indicators; wire services (AP, Reuters) publish reaction stories within minutes of the 8:30 a.m. release.
- **Financial markets:** the advance retail sales report is a **regularly market-moving event**; academics have documented significant stock and Treasury futures reactions (and even some evidence of informed pre-announcement drift, studied in an ECB working paper), and the release is protected by lockup-room procedures. Currency, bond, and equity traders treat the headline and the "control group" (sales ex-auto, gas, building materials, food services — the slice that maps to PCE) as key inputs.

---

## 10. Benefits to the Public

- **Timeliness:** Without MARTS, the earliest official measure of retail sales would arrive ~40 days after the reference month; MARTS delivers it in roughly half that time. This is its raison d'être — the survey exists specifically because users demanded a faster read.
- **Earliest official read on consumer demand:** Retail sales are "one of the primary measures of consumer demand for both durable and non-durable goods"; consumer spending drives roughly two-thirds to 70% of U.S. GDP, so this single release shapes GDP nowcasts, Fed policy expectations, and public understanding of the economy.
- **Foundation of the national accounts:** Feeds directly into GDP/PCE estimation, benchmarking, and input-output tables — so even citizens who never look at the release are affected by it through economic policy and statistics.
- **Policy evaluation:** Census's FAQ notes the survey "provides reliable measures of current economic activity that are essential to an objective assessment of the need for, and impact of," economic policy.
- **Free and open access:** All outputs are public domain (U.S. federal government work), free, with full methodology disclosure, replicable seasonal adjustment, published confidence intervals, and multiple machine-readable access routes (API, Excel/CSV, FRED/ALFRED).
- **Low respondent burden:** The subsample design (~4,800 of ~13,000 firms), certainty-unit rotation, and 2–3 year redesigns deliberately limit and rotate burden on small businesses — a good example of burden-conscious survey design under the Paperwork Reduction Act.

---

## 11. Quality, Reliability, and Known Limitations

- **Accuracy:** The **average absolute revision to the advance estimate is roughly two-tenths of one percent** — remarkably small for a first estimate.
- **Statistical transparency:** Each release includes 90% confidence intervals and asterisks when the interval includes zero (insufficient evidence the change differs from zero). Variances come from random-groups methods.
- **Limitations to flag for users:**
  - National only — no subnational geography.
  - Nominal dollars — not inflation-adjusted; analysts deflating with CPI/BLS measures must do so themselves.
  - Voluntary response and no imputation for most nonrespondents (handled via the link-relative estimator).
  - No business births between sample redesigns (up to ~3 years).
  - Time-series breaks: April 2025 nonemployer removal; periodic NAICS reclassifications; annual/5-year benchmark revisions.
  - Some months are statistical zeros (e.g., October 2025: +0.0%*, September 2025: +0.2%*) — the asterisk convention matters for interpretation.
  - Shutdown-related delays (2019, 2025) create irregular release lags and possibly affected collection quality in those periods.

---

## 12. Current Status (as of this writing)

- The most recent release: **August 2026** advance estimates — $773.9 billion (SA), **up 1.2% (±0.4) m/m, up 6.0% (±0.5) y/y**; July 2026 was revised to $763.6 billion (−0.6% m/m). Next release: September 2026 data on **October 15, 2026**, with subsequent releases running monthly through December 2026.
- The survey remains active, with no planned methodology changes announced in the August 2025 OMB clearance notice ("Currently, there are no planned changes for MARTS").

---

## 13. Key Sources Consulted

- Census Bureau, MARTS methodology: https://www.census.gov/retail/marts/how_surveys_are_collected.html
- Census Bureau, About the Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey: https://www.census.gov/retail/marts/about_the_surveys.html
- Census Bureau, historical MARTS releases (1953–present): https://www.census.gov/retail/marts/historic_releases.html
- Census Bureau, release schedule: https://www.census.gov/retail/release_schedule.html
- Federal Register, Monthly Retail Surveys OMB clearance (Aug. 5, 2025): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/05/2025-14783/ (and 2023-00622; 2012-15525)
- OMB Supporting Statement, MARTS Part B: https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/DownloadDocument?objectID=32987701
- Recent releases: https://www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/adv2510.pdf (Oct 2025, shutdown-delayed), https://www2.census.gov/marts/adv2408.pdf
- BEA NIPA Handbook, Chapter 3 (principal source data): https://www.bea.gov/resources/methodologies/nipa-handbook/pdf/chapter-03.pdf
- FRED release page: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=9; ALFRED vintage archive: https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/release?rid=9
- Chicago Fed CARTS (MARTS-benchmarked weekly nowcast): https://www.chicagofed.org/research/data/carts/current-data
- Reuters (via KELO and TradingView) on the 43-day October–November 2025 shutdown's impact on the retail sales release.

**Bottom line:** MARTS is a small (~4,800-firm), voluntary, high-leverage survey whose sole purpose is speed: it buys the nation roughly three weeks of additional timeliness on the single most-watched measure of consumer demand, feeding GDP estimates, monetary policy deliberations, and market pricing — and it comes with a deep, well-preserved (if occasionally revised) 70-plus-year public archive.

# Dataset Risk Assessment: Advance Monthly Sales for Retail and Food Services Survey (MARTS)

**Assessment date:** October 8, 2026
**Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce)
**OMB ICR:** 0607-0717 (Monthly Retail Surveys, combined MRTS+MARTS; formerly 0607-0104)

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**

- *For "No Known Issue":* The full press-release archive (December 1953–present) remains available at www2.census.gov/retail/releases/historical/marts/, and time-series data remain accessible via the Census economic time-series tool (program code MARTS), FRED, and ALFRED (which preserves as-first-released vintages).
- *For "Moderate Risk":* In the **April 2025 annual revision, nonemployer (no-paid-employee) firm estimates were removed from the entire published MARTS/MRTS time series** to align with the Annual Integrated Economic Survey. This means data elements that existed in prior-cycle data (coverage of nonemployer sales, roughly the gap between the old and new series) were removed/redefined retroactively on the primary location. Separately, in **early February 2025, Census FTP downloads (www2.census.gov — the host of the MARTS archive) returned "403 Forbidden" errors for several days** following the administration's gender-ideology executive order compliance; NPR/GPB reported over 3,000 Census pages removed (mostly research/methodology pages), later largely restored. This was a temporary removal affecting access to historical files, driven by a presidential action.
- *For "High Risk"/"Gone":* No evidence of permanent removal of MARTS data files; the historical archive is intact.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The pre-2025 nonemployer-inclusive series — an element of the dataset that existed for prior cycles — was removed from the primary publication as of the April 2025 revision, and the February 2025 outage (administration-EO-driven) temporarily blocked access to the historical archive. The files themselves survive (with ALFRED preserving old vintages), so this does not rise to "High Risk," but the retroactive redefinition is a genuine, documented alteration of prior-cycle data.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**

- *For "No Known Issue":* The ICR was **renewed before expiration**: OMB approved the Monthly Retail Surveys extension (ICR 202511-0607-002) on **April 6, 2026**, ahead of the April 30, 2026 expiration, with a new expiration of **April 30, 2029**. The 2026 release calendar is published and running; releases since April 2026 have been back on schedule (e.g., August 2026 data released September 16, 2026; September 2026 due October 15, 2026), and the 2027 calendar already lists January–February 2027 dates. Collection and publication have not been terminated.
- *For "Moderate Risk":* The **43-day October–November 2025 government shutdown (longest in history) halted collection, processing, and publication**. The September 2025 advance report, due October 16, 2025, was released **November 25, 2025** (~40 days late); October 2025 was released December 16, 2025; November 2025 on January 14, 2026; and the catch-up schedule pushed every release roughly 3–6 weeks late until the April 2026 report, after which Reuters confirmed the Bureau "caught up" and releases resumed on time. This squarely constitutes "typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed."
- *For "High Risk":* No statutory publication deadline was permanently missed, no collection was skipped entirely (all reference months were ultimately published), and the ICR never lapsed.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Publication of multiple reference months (September 2025–March 2026) was significantly delayed by the shutdown, and collection was suspended for over a month. However, the ICR is active through 2029, no data month was skipped, and the series is fully caught up. The pattern (2019 and 2025 shutdowns both caused delays) suggests recurring but recoverable disruption.

## Data Quality

**Evidence:**

- *For "No Known Issue":* No announced reduction in granularity, timeliness, or frequency. The ICR renewal was an "extension without change" of collection; burden (156,000 responses; 18,200 hours) is unchanged. The survey continues monthly with its full industry detail, e-commerce estimates, confidence intervals, and its ~9–12 business-day timeliness. Average absolute revision remains ~0.2%.
- *For "Moderate Risk":* (1) The **April 2025 nonemployer redefinition reduced the coverage scope** of the series (employer firms only), a conceptual narrowing of what "retail sales" measures, executed retroactively across the time series — a coverage change users must handle. (2) **Staffing losses (~10–15% agency-wide, ~1,300–1,500 employees), a government-wide hiring freeze, and field-staff shortages** are documented risks to data collection capacity; Commerce IG found Census "lacks effective strategies to address staffing gaps"; AMSTAT's *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025* flags operational constraints from hiring freezes and a backlog of 3,000+ contract approvals. (3) The shutdown forced a suspension of collection for the October 2025 reference month, with unknown effects on response quality for that period. (4) A further revision incorporating the 2023–2024 AIES results is scheduled for September 28, 2026, continuing the series-redefinition process.
- *For "High Risk":* No actual reduction in the indicator's granularity, frequency, or (post-shutdown) timeliness has occurred, unlike, e.g., BLS's CPI sample reductions during 2025. The FY2026 budget request held Current Economic Statistics flat at $216 million, signaling protection of the economic indicator programs specifically.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The indicator itself has maintained its granularity and cadence, but the retroactive coverage redefinition, the shutdown-era collection suspension, and agency-wide staffing/hiring-freeze pressures constitute a real, documented, and ongoing (not merely hypothetical) risk to quality — though short of an actual reduction in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence:**

- *For "No Known Issue":* The collection operates under **explicitly named statutory authority: 13 U.S.C. §§ 131 and 182** (cited on the reginfo ICR record), with confidentiality protections under 13 U.S.C. § 9. It is an **OMB-designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator** and is **required for implementation of federal programs**: the BEA uses MARTS/MRTS estimates as a principal source for the PCE component of GDP (the advance report feeds BEA's advance GDP estimate) and to benchmark annual input-output tables — explicitly stated in the ICR abstract itself. The FY2026 budget justification explicitly defends Current Economic Statistics as supporting "GDP estimation, fiscal and monetary policymaking, and private sector decision making." No alternative federal collection provides monthly, ~10-day-lag retail sales estimates.
- *For "Moderate Risk":* MARTS is not *mandated* by statute (no statute orders a monthly advance retail survey; response is voluntary). One could argue MRTS — the parent survey that publishes the same concept one month later — is an alternative collection that serves as a substitute (indeed it formally supersedes MARTS estimates each month).
- *For "High Risk":* Not applicable — authorization is not vague, programmatic use is extensively documented (BEA, Federal Reserve, CEA), and no timely substitute exists in the federal statistical system.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Statutory authorization is explicitly named (13 U.S.C. 131/182), the survey is required for implementation of a federal program (BEA's national accounts/GDP estimation, per the ICR record itself), and it holds PFEI status with documented, irreplaceable programmatic use. The MRTS overlap provides a lagged, not timely, substitute — the timeliness is the entire product — so the "alternative substitute" concern doesn't materially apply. This is the dataset's strongest protective factor.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**

- *For "High Risk":* The Census Bureau has **lost approximately 1,300–1,500 employees since January 2025** through deferred resignations (a DOGE-initiated program), voluntary separations, early retirements, and RIFs — AFGE Council 241 president Johnny Zuagar cited ~1,500; AP reported ~1,300 — out of ~13,230 employees as of September 2024. **This exceeds the rubric's absolute threshold of 1,000+ staff lost**, even though the percentage (~10–15%, per AMSTAT) sits at the low end. In October 2025, ~100 Census employees at the Tucson call center received RIF notices ("lack of funds"); parent agency Commerce laid off ~300. **Leadership has been removed/destabilized:** Senate-confirmed Director Rob Santos resigned in early 2025; COO Ron Jarmin served in an acting capacity; political appointee George Cook was named acting director in September 2025 — the Bureau has had **no Senate-confirmed director throughout the assessment period**, and AP reported 18 vacancies among top leaders.
- *For "Moderate Risk":* Percentage-wise the loss is 10–15%, and the **budget was not cut 20%** — in fact the enacted FY2026 CJS appropriations (P.L. 119-74) gave Census **$1.490 billion, a $108 million increase** over FY2024/25. The Current Surveys and Programs account took a modest cut ($329M enacted FY24/25 → $319M enacted FY26, ~3%), and the administration's proposed $289M (~12% cut, targeting SIPP and demographic statistics) was **rejected by Congress**. Current Economic Statistics specifically was held flat at $216 million.
- *For "No Known Issue":* Not supportable — the staff losses and leadership changes are well documented.

**Finding: High Risk.** Although the percentage of staff lost (10–15%) and the enacted budget (a slight increase) would suggest "Moderate Risk," the rubric's absolute criterion — "1,000 or more staff lost" — is clearly met, and the agency has operated without confirmed leadership under a political-appointee acting director. Mitigating factor worth noting: the funding line that pays for MARTS (Current Economic Statistics) was protected at flat funding in both the request and the enacted bill, and final FY2026 law excluded a House provision that would have limited follow-up contacts across all surveys.

## Policy

**Evidence:**

- *For "No Known Issue":* No presidential action specifically targets MARTS or retail sales data; the ICR renewal was a routine PRA process ("extension without change"), not a presidential-action-driven ICR. The FY2026 budget justification explicitly praises the economic statistics programs. No negative policy note about retail sales appears on the Census site. The nonemployer redefinition was a methodological alignment with the AIES that predates the current administration (AIES launched with reference year 2022).
- *For "Moderate Risk":* Several **proposed or pending changes** bear on the agency: (1) the President's Budget **proposes reorganizing BLS, BEA, and Census within Commerce** (status/timeline unspecified); (2) the FY2026 request directs Census to **eliminate functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission"** by end of FY2026, with no detail — a test MARTS would likely pass given § 131/182 authority, but which has already claimed other survey programs (e.g., USDA terminated the CPS Food Security Supplement); (3) **DOGE has explicitly targeted the Census Bureau** (AP), and the acting director is a political appointee installed alongside an unprecedented presidential order reshaping the decennial census — evidence of heightened political direction of the agency; (4) the February 2025 website/data removals, while temporary and not MARTS-specific, demonstrated that administration EOs can take Census data offline; (5) the administration-driven workforce reductions described above. Related agencies show the pattern of policy-driven cuts reaching economic data (BLS CPI sample reductions).
- *For "High Risk":* No evidence of a presidential-action-driven change to what MARTS collects or publishes, no negative policy note on the site, and no MARTS-specific change made "in accordance with Administration priorities."

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** The changes actually implemented that touch this dataset (website takedown, staffing attrition, shutdown delays) were collateral effects of administration actions rather than targeted policy changes to MARTS, and the economic-indicator programs have been rhetorically and fiscally protected. But pending proposals (statistical-agency reorganization, elimination of "non-mandated" functions, DOGE review of surveys) and agency leadership politicization mean changes affecting this data are plausibly "being considered" — the textbook definition of Moderate Risk.

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** — nonemployer data elements removed retroactively from the time series (April 2025); temporary administration-EO-driven archive outage (Feb 2025); files otherwise intact since 1953 |
| **Future Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** — publication dates missed for Sept 2025–Mar 2026 due to the 43-day shutdown; ICR renewed on time (active through 04/30/2029); releases now back on schedule |
| **Data Quality** | **Moderate Risk** — granularity/frequency maintained, but coverage redefined, collection suspended during shutdown, and staffing/hiring-freeze pressures documented |
| **Statutory Context** | **No Known Issue** — explicit authority (13 U.S.C. 131/182), PFEI status, required for BEA's GDP/PCE program, no timely substitute exists |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **High Risk** — 1,300–1,500 staff lost (meets the 1,000+ threshold), RIFs during shutdown, no Senate-confirmed director, political-appointee acting director (budget itself was not cut) |
| **Policy** | **Moderate Risk** — no targeted action against MARTS and economic statistics explicitly protected in budget documents, but pending reorganization of the statistical agencies, DOGE scrutiny, and a directive to eliminate non-mandated functions create genuine pending-change risk |

**Overall assessment:** MARTS is comparatively well-protected among federal datasets — its statutory footing, PFEI status, GDP-estimation role, market-moving profile, and flat-funded budget line make it a poor candidate for termination, and its 70+ year archive (with ALFRED vintage preservation as a backup) is secure. The realistic near-term risks are (1) staffing-driven degradation of collection quality, (2) recurring shutdown-driven release delays (2019, 2025), and (3) collateral damage from agency-wide reorganization or website-compliance actions, rather than deliberate removal.
